questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the real difference between `var` and `let` in JavaScript?
options: `var` is function-scoped, so a variable declared inside an `if` block with `var` remains accessible outside that block within the same function; `let` is block-scoped and does not
`var` and `let` behave identically except for stylistic preference
`let` allows reassignment while `var` does not
`var` throws a ReferenceError when referenced before its declaration line, while `let` returns `undefined`
questions.explain: Lesson 1 shows exactly this: a `var` declared inside an `if` block stays accessible throughout the whole function, while a `let` declared the same way only exists inside that block.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D has the real behavior backwards. `var` is hoisted and silently returns `undefined` when referenced before its declaration line; `let`/`const` are the ones that throw a real error when referenced too early, because the variable exists in the block but isn't usable yet.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `typeof null` returns the string "________", a quirk baked into JavaScript since 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking the entire web.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 calls this out directly: `typeof null` returns `"object"`, not `"null"` -- when you need to specifically detect null, compare the value directly with `=== null` instead of relying on `typeof`.

questions.prompt: What does this log when called as `checkPriority(2)`?
options: undefined -- the if-block never ran, but `message` is still declared (hoisted) throughout the whole function
ReferenceError: message is not defined
Critical
A SyntaxError, because message is used before being assigned a value
questions.explain: Lesson 1's core point about `var`: it is function-scoped and hoisted, so `message` exists for the whole function even though the `if` block that would have assigned it never ran -- it just never gets a value, so it logs `undefined`.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about `.forEach()`, `.map()`, `.filter()`, and `.indexOf()` as taught in this course.
options: .map() returns a brand-new array, leaving the original array unchanged
.forEach() returns a brand-new transformed array, just like .map() does
.filter() returns a new array containing only the items for which the callback returned true
.indexOf() returns -1 when a value is not found in the array
.push() returns a new array with the added item, leaving the original array unchanged
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit: .map() and .filter() each return a new array and leave the original alone; .forEach() runs a function per item but returns nothing useful; .indexOf() returns -1 when nothing matches; .push() mutates the original array in place and returns the new length, not a new array.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from the Fundamentals Lab's filter-then-map pattern in the correct order, from first to last.
items: Trace through the ticket data by hand to know the expected answer before writing any code
Use .filter() to keep only tickets that are priority 1 and unassigned
Use .map() to transform the filtered tickets into just their ticket numbers
Run the function and confirm the result matches the hand-traced expectation
questions.explain: Lesson 6 walks this exact sequence: trace by hand first so you know the expected answer, filter for the compound condition, map to pull out just the numbers, then run it and confirm the result matches the trace.

questions.prompt: A developer says: "Our instance is on a recent release, so I can finally rewrite GlideRecord itself to use modern syntax." What's actually wrong with that statement?
options: The GraalVM migration changed which JavaScript syntax the engine accepts, not the Glide API objects themselves -- GlideRecord's method names and behavior are unchanged
GlideRecord was removed entirely as part of the GraalVM migration
Modern ServiceNow instances no longer support any ES5 syntax at all
GlideRecord now requires Promises instead of while(gr.next()) loops
questions.explain: Lesson 7 draws this exact boundary: the engine's syntax moved forward (let/const, template literals are now valid), but the API surface -- GlideRecord, gs, GlideDateTime -- was deliberately left untouched so existing scripts keep running unchanged.

questions.prompt: Without changing anything else, rewriting the inner callback below as a(n) ________ function is the standard fix for the `this` bug, because that kind of function has no `this` of its own and inherits it lexically from `logEach`.
questions.explain: Lesson 8 shows exactly this bug and its fix: rewriting the .forEach() callback as an arrow function makes it inherit `this` lexically from `logEach`, where `this` correctly refers to `utils`.

questions.prompt: Match each term from this chapter to what it actually does.
right: Converts a JSON-formatted string into a real JavaScript object
ServiceNow's own date/time object, aware of the instance's and user's configured time zones
Converts a JavaScript object into a JSON-formatted string
Advances a GlideDateTime by a number of days, computed in UTC for timezone safety
questions.explain: Lessons 9 and 10 cover each of these: GlideDateTime exists because native Date doesn't know the instance's or user's time zone; addDaysUTC() moves a GlideDateTime forward safely; JSON.parse() turns a string into an object; JSON.stringify() turns an object into a string.

questions.prompt: Inside a Scripted REST API resource script, what's wrong with reading `.priority` directly off the raw request body like this?
questions.code:
var requestBody = request.body.dataString;
var priority = requestBody.priority; // <-- this line
options: requestBody is still a plain string at this point -- it must be passed through JSON.parse() first before .priority can be read as a real property
request.body.dataString never actually contains a priority field
Scripted REST APIs can only receive XML, never JSON
.priority must be accessed with JSON.stringify() instead of dot notation
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is explicit about this: even though a JSON string looks like an object, it is just text until JSON.parse() converts it into a real JavaScript object with actual readable properties.

questions.prompt: What does a `GlideRecord` object actually represent before `.query()` or `.get()` is called?
options: A cursor positioned over a table, capable of walking through matching rows one at a time, but holding no data until queried
An in-memory copy of every row currently in the table
A single record already loaded from the database, ready to read its fields immediately
A SQL string that must be manually executed with gs.sql() before it does anything
questions.explain: Lesson 12 is explicit: a GlideRecord isn't one loaded row, it's a cursor that knows how to ask a table questions. Creating `new GlideRecord('incident')` doesn't fetch a single row -- nothing happens against the database until you call .query() or .get().
questions.distractorExplain: Option C is the closest wrong answer because it's true *after* a successful .get() or .query()+.next() -- but it's false at the moment the GlideRecord is first constructed, which is what the question actually asks about. Right after `new GlideRecord('incident')`, no row has been fetched yet.

questions.prompt: How are the two .addQuery() conditions below combined, and what happens the first time .next() is called after .query()?
options: They combine with AND by default, and the first .next() call advances the cursor onto the first matching row, returning true
They combine with OR by default, and .next() must be called twice before any row is available
They combine with AND, but the cursor is already positioned on the first row immediately after .query(), before .next() is ever called
They combine with AND, and .next() returns the field values of the first row directly, rather than a boolean
questions.explain: Lesson 13 is explicit: multiple .addQuery() calls combine with AND by default, and .next() both advances the cursor and returns true/false -- right after .query() the cursor isn't on any row yet, so the first .next() call is what moves it onto the first result.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: after `gr.initialize()` and `gr.setValue()` calls build up a new record in memory, calling `gr.________()` actually saves the row and returns its new sys_id.
questions.explain: Lesson 14's insert pattern: initialize() sets up a blank in-memory record, setValue() fills in fields, and .insert() is the call that actually saves the row and returns the new sys_id (or null on failure).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about deleting records with GlideRecord.
options: .deleteRecord() deletes only the one record the cursor is currently positioned on, and requires .next() to have found it first
.deleteMultiple() deletes every record matching the current query in one operation, with no while(gr.next()) loop required
.deleteMultiple() asks for row-by-row confirmation before deleting each matching record
.deleteRecord() and .deleteMultiple() are interchangeable and always delete the exact same set of records
A query broader than intended makes .deleteMultiple() more dangerous, since there's no per-row confirmation step
questions.explain: Lesson 14 covers exactly this: .deleteRecord() removes the one currently-positioned record and needs .next() first; .deleteMultiple() removes everything matching the query at once, with no loop and no row-by-row confirmation, which is exactly why a too-broad query is dangerous with it.

questions.prompt: What does this query actually find?
options: Active incidents where priority is 1 OR 2 -- the OR condition group is itself ANDed with active=true
All incidents regardless of priority, as long as they are active OR priority 1 OR 2
Only incidents where priority is exactly 1, ignoring the addOrCondition entirely
An error, because addOrCondition cannot be chained onto addQuery's return value
questions.explain: Lesson 15 explains this exact pattern: chaining .addOrCondition() onto .addQuery()'s return value creates "priority 1 OR priority 2" as one combined condition group, which is then still ANDed with every other .addQuery() call on the same GlideRecord, like active == true.

questions.prompt: The GlideRecord Lab's `reassignStaleP1s` method finds every open, unassigned Priority 1 incident older than 24 hours, reassigns each one, and returns how many it reassigned. Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Compute the 24-hour cutoff once with gs.hoursAgo(24), outside any loop
Build one GlideRecord query combining active, priority, the null assigned_to check, and the created-before-cutoff condition
Call .query() once to send the combined filter to the database
Loop with while(gr.next()), setting the new assignment group and calling .update() on each matching row, incrementing a counter
Return the counter as the number of incidents actually reassigned
questions.explain: Lesson 17 traces this exact order: compute the cutoff once, combine all four conditions into a single query, send it once with .query(), update each matching row inside one loop while counting, then return the count -- avoiding every Lesson 16 pitfall (no N+1, no wasted getRowCount, no missing limit where a limit would be wrong).

questions.prompt: Why can't a Client Script just reference GlideRecord directly to query a table?
options: GlideRecord is a server-side class that doesn't exist in the browser's JavaScript at all, and letting the browser query the database directly would bypass server-side ACL checks
GlideRecord exists in the browser but is disabled by default for performance reasons
GlideRecord only works inside Scheduled Jobs, never inside any other script type
Client Scripts can use GlideRecord, but only under a different method name
questions.explain: Lesson 18 is explicit: GlideRecord is a server-side class and doesn't exist in the browser at all. The server is the only place database access can be checked against ACLs on every call, which is exactly why the browser can only ask through GlideAjax, never query directly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: any Script Include that GlideAjax is going to call must extend ServiceNow's built-in `________` class -- without it, the Script Include cannot be a GlideAjax target at all, no matter how else it's configured.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 names the real base class: extending AbstractAjaxProcessor is what wires a Script Include into the GlideAjax request/response plumbing in the first place; a regular Script Include that doesn't extend it can never be called by GlideAjax.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about making a Script Include callable from GlideAjax.
options: The Script Include record's "Client callable" checkbox must be checked, and it is unchecked by default
A method whose name starts with an underscore is never reachable from the client, even on a client-callable Script Include
Extending AbstractAjaxProcessor alone is enough, even if "Client callable" is left unchecked
this.getParameter('sysparm_x') reads a value the client sent via addParam('sysparm_x', value)
Every method on a client-callable Script Include automatically becomes reachable from the client
questions.explain: Lesson 19 lays out both requirements together: extending AbstractAjaxProcessor is necessary but not sufficient -- Client callable must also be checked -- and an underscore-prefixed method stays private even then, so not every method is automatically exposed.

questions.prompt: Put the GlideAjax round trip in the correct order, from the user's action to the result landing back on the form.
items: A Client Script constructs a GlideAjax object and names the method to call with sysparm_name
The browser sends an asynchronous request to the server naming the Script Include and method
The named method runs on the server, with full GlideRecord access, and builds a result
A callback function in the Client Script receives the result once the server responds and updates the form
questions.explain: Lesson 18 lays out this exact four-step round trip: only the server-side step ever touches the database; the browser's role is asking the question and later reading the answer inside the callback.

questions.prompt: What actually happens every single time this onSubmit script runs?
options: The save always proceeds, because the GlideAjax callback is asynchronous and hasn't run yet by the time `return !isBlocked` executes
The save is always blocked, regardless of what the server answers
The script throws an error, because getXMLAnswer cannot be used inside onSubmit
The save correctly waits for the server's answer before returning
questions.explain: Lesson 24 walks through exactly this broken pattern: the callback runs later, after onSubmit has already returned, so isBlocked is still false every time regardless of the real answer -- silently defeating the validation.

questions.prompt: Match each g_form method to what it actually does.
right: Hides the field entirely from the form
Toggles the red asterisk and the save-time requirement on
Posts a banner styled to draw attention, explaining why a save is being blocked
Locks the field so the user can see it but not edit it
questions.explain: Lesson 22 covers all four: setMandatory toggles the required asterisk, setReadOnly locks editing while keeping the field visible, setVisible shows or hides it entirely, and addErrorMessage posts the attention-drawing banner used to explain a blocked save.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: returning `________` from an onSubmit Client Script blocks the save entirely, leaving the record open and unsaved exactly as the user left it.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 states this as the one critical difference for onSubmit: returning false actually blocks the save, while returning true (or nothing) lets it proceed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ServiceNow's three Client Script types.
options: onLoad runs once, right after the form finishes loading
onChange receives oldValue and newValue as real parameters
onSubmit is the only one of the three whose return value matters
If a form has two onSubmit scripts and only one of them returns false, the record still saves
isLoading matters inside onChange to avoid firing real logic while the form is still populating
questions.explain: Lesson 23 covers each of these: onLoad fires once after loading, onChange gets oldValue/newValue, only onSubmit's return value is checked, and isLoading guards onChange from firing during initial load. A single false from any onSubmit script blocks the save -- the record does NOT save in that scenario, so option D is false.

questions.prompt: A Business Rule is configured to run asynchronously, queued to execute later outside your session. Why can't the Script Debugger help troubleshoot it?
options: The Script Debugger only attaches to synchronous execution you personally trigger while attached to your session, not to scripts running later with no session attached
The Script Debugger only works on Client Scripts, never on Business Rules
Asynchronous Business Rules don't run any server-side JavaScript at all
The Script Debugger requires the Business Rule to have zero breakpoints set
questions.explain: Lesson 26 states the Script Debugger's real limit directly: it debugs synchronous, session-attached execution. An asynchronous Business Rule runs later, outside your session, so there's nothing for the debugger to pause -- which is exactly why Lesson 27's gs.info()/System Log workflow exists.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every gs.info(), gs.warn(), gs.error(), and the older gs.log() call writes a row into the `________` table -- the same System Log table already queryable with GlideRecord.
questions.explain: Lesson 27 is explicit: gs.info() isn't a special debugging-only channel -- every one of these calls writes a row into the syslog table, the same System Log table you already know how to query.

questions.prompt: This encoded query silently returns zero rows instead of throwing an error. Why?
options: ServiceNow's encoded query parser doesn't validate the value 'ture' -- it simply never matches any record, because no record has a literal active value of 'ture'
The ^ operator is invalid syntax here and should be ^OR
addEncodedQuery() requires its field names to be listed in alphabetical order
risk is not a valid field on the change_request table
questions.explain: Lesson 29's debugging lab finds exactly this typo: 'active=ture' doesn't throw an error, it just never matches any record, since no record actually has that literal value -- a silent query failure that a row-count gs.info() catches immediately.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from the Debugging Lab's workflow in the correct order for diagnosing the ChangeRequestUtils bug.
items: Add a gs.info() right after .query() to log how many rows actually came back
Read the System Log, filtered to that source, and see the row count is zero
Re-examine the encoded query string and find the active=ture typo
Re-run the same gs.info() trace to confirm the row count is no longer zero
questions.explain: Lesson 29 walks this exact sequence: confirm the query is even finding records first, read the log to rule out the loop/return logic, locate the actual typo, fix it, then verify the fix instead of just assuming it worked.

questions.prompt: Match each TaskUtils method from the capstone to its actual purpose.
right: Checks group membership via GlideRecord, using setLimit(1) to stop at the first match
The thin client-callable wrapper that reads sysparm_ parameters and delegates to the real method
Returns a reference field's human-readable text, defensively, after checking the field is valid
Returns a display-ready string, flagging a date as overdue using GlideDateTime.before()
questions.explain: Lessons 30-31 define each method exactly this way: isUserInGroup does the real GlideRecord membership check with setLimit(1); formatDueDate flags overdue dates with before(); getReferenceDisplayValue defensively reads a display value; ajaxIsUserInGroup is the thin wrapper that reads getParameter() calls and delegates to isUserInGroup.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the code review performed on the finished TaskUtils class.
options: isUserInGroup's membership query uses setLimit(1) so it stops at the first matching row instead of scanning the whole table
getReferenceDisplayValue calls gs.info() on every single call, logging every lookup
Neither GlideRecord query inside TaskUtils sits inside a loop
Every comparison inside TaskUtils itself uses === rather than ==
isUserInGroup throws an unhandled exception if userId or groupName is missing
questions.explain: Lesson 32's review confirms setLimit(1) is used, neither query sits in a loop, and every comparison is strict (===). getReferenceDisplayValue logs gs.info() only on the exception path, not on every call, and isUserInGroup defensively returns false on missing input rather than throwing.

questions.prompt: The code review flags `answer == 'true'` as a risk in the Client Script calling TaskUtils's GlideAjax wrapper, but accepts `answer === 'true'`. Why?
options: GlideAjax always returns its answer as a string, and === only matches the exact string 'true', while == could loosely coerce-match other truthy-looking values in ways that mask a bug
== runs measurably slower than === in every JavaScript engine
GlideAjax answers are returned as native booleans, so == would always fail by comparing a boolean to a string
=== is only valid syntax inside Script Includes, never inside Client Scripts
questions.explain: Lesson 32 explains this directly: the GlideAjax answer is always a string, so === only matches the exact string "true", while == could loosely match other values in ways that mask a real bug -- the same strict-equality discipline from Chapter 1 applied to a real GlideAjax callback.
